title: The country parson
hook: George Herbert on the pastor who visits, teaches and prays through the ordinary

segments.voice: Yesterday, evensong: Mary's song and Simeon's, sung as the light goes. Your line was the day ends in song. What was the last song of your day? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five.

A small book with a long title: A Priest to the Temple, or, The Country Parson. Its author, George Herbert, was a poet and a priest of the Church of England who served a small country parish. In short chapters he sets down what a good pastor does: how he lives, how he preaches, how he comforts, how he runs his house. One chapter follows him out the door on an ordinary weekday afternoon, walking from house to house. Not on Sunday, when everyone is ready for him. On a plain weekday, when nobody is. Today: the country parson.

Herbert's reason for the weekday visit is simple, and a little sly. On Sunday, people come to church dressed up and on their best behavior. On a weekday afternoon the parson finds them as they really are, in the middle of their work and their troubles, and that's where he can actually help. So he goes from house to house: comforting the sick, praising the hard-working, admonishing the idle, giving to those in need, and, where it's welcome, praying with them right there among the pots and tools. The Bible behind this is plain. In Jesus's picture of the last judgment, the king says, "I was sick, and ye visited me." The letter of James puts it even more bluntly: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction." In James's words, visiting belongs to pure religion. Herbert's poems say the same thing from the inside. In one called The Elixir, he asks God to teach him to see God in all things, and then he lands here: "Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, / Makes that and th' action fine." Sweeping. Not a vision, not a cathedral. A broom. That is the Anglican way Herbert sketches: holiness found in the ordinary parish, the ordinary week, the ordinary room. Not every Christian has a parson. Some have a pastor, a priest, an elder, the leader of a small group, or a neighbor who simply shows up. But the picture travels well: someone who knows the street, knocks on the door, and sits down at the kitchen table in the middle of the mess.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.`
`WHO SWEEPS A ROOM, AS FOR THY LAWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one visit. Sit and let your breathing settle. Let a face come to mind: someone sick, someone alone, someone you haven't sat with in a while. Don't build a speech. Just see yourself knocking, being let in, sitting down in the middle of whatever their day is. What could you bring? Soup, a card, an hour. If a visit isn't possible, a call counts. If you pray, you can hold that person before God now, by name. The bell holds the time.
The country parson. George Herbert's picture of a pastor who lives among his people, visits them on ordinary days, and finds God in ordinary work.

Your line: the ordinary parish. Today, visit someone, at their door or on the phone, on a plain weekday. This week ran from the Celtic circle and the oarless boat to the prayer book's two hinges, evensong, and now a knock at the door. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: In parish life, Anglican clergy and lay visitors call on the sick, the housebound and the grieving at home, and some clergy still read Herbert's The Country Parson as a picture of a pastor's work.

fork.reveal: Herbert sends the parson out on weekday afternoons. on Sunday people are on their best behavior; on a weekday he finds them as they are, and can help.

original.note: Greek: to look in on, to visit and care for — the verb behind "visit" in James 1:27 and Matthew 25:36.

what a scholar hears: the Greek verb James uses for visit is also the one in Matthew 25:36, "ye visited me": looking in on someone who needs care.

notes: The Country Parson, ch. 14 ('The Parson in Circuit'): Herbert sends the parson visiting on weekday afternoons because then he finds people as they are, 'wallowing in the midst of their affairs', whereas on Sundays they are dressed and composed. Paraphrased; confirm the paraphrase and the list of what he does on visits (comforting, exhorting, reproving, giving, praying), which is a summary.
Biographical detail is kept minimal: 'a poet and a priest of the Church of England who served a small country parish' (Bemerton, near Salisbury). No dates or ages given.

The Elixir quotation follows the 1633 text as usually printed ('Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, / Makes that and th' action fine'). Confirm spelling; translation field marked 'public domain (original)' since it is English verse.
Original: ἐπισκέπτομαι; James 1:27 has ἐπισκέπτεσθαι and Matthew 25:36 ἐπεσκέψασθε. Confirm the gloss 'to look in on, to visit and care for'.

Editor pass: 'In James's book, visiting is religion' overstated James 1:27 (which also names keeping unspotted from the world); now 'visiting belongs to pure religion', and the matching screen line quotes the verse instead. Trapdoor's lexical claim ('not just to drop by') replaced with the shared verb in James 1:27 and Matthew 25:36.

Audit (2026-10-02): 'settling quarrels' is not in ch. 14 (reconciling neighbors is elsewhere in the book); replaced with 'praising the hard-working, admonishing the idle', which ch. 14 does describe. 'Comforting the sick' is ch. 15; confirm the summary.
